steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a game theory / algorithms paper where we give a polynomial-time algorithm for computing a Nash equilibrium in the attack-and-defense network game of Bloch, Chatterjee and Dutta. Motivate the setting, summarize their model and the open question, describe our approach, and cover related work on network interdiction and equilibrium computation.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There are many situations where strategic actors interact over a network of bilateral connections, for example international drug trafficking, disrupting the movement of the enemy troops, and terrorist attacks. One class of such scenarios is when there is a network of defenders (for example countries that are connected by common borders) and an attacker who tries to move an undesirable object (like a bomb or a package of drugs) through the network to a targeted node (like a targeted country). Each defender cares about his own security, but when he invests in protection this spills over to the defenders that come after him on the potential routes of attack.

Bloch, Chatterjee, and Dutta recently introduced a game theoretic model that captures these scenarios. In the model there is an attacker (node 0) and n defenders, and they are all connected in a fixed network. The attacker chooses a target node and also an attack path in the network that goes from her location (node 0) to the location of the targeted node. If the attack is successful, the attacker gains the value that is assigned to the target node. The targeted defender loses his value if he is successfully attacked, and every other node on the path stays intact. To prevent potential losses, every defender can invest in protection, which is costly, to increase the probability of stopping a potential attack. Every defender on the attack path can stop the attack. Bloch et al. show that mixed strategy Nash equilibria (NE) exist in the model, and they get a partial characterization of the NE and a full characterization when the network is a line. They prove that the set of nodes that are attacked with positive probability in NE is unique, and that under a certain redefinition the model has a unique NE. They give a set of non-linear equations that describe the strategies in a NE when the set of nodes attacked with positive probability is given. But it was left open whether this set can be computed efficiently, and so whether a NE of the model can be computed efficiently.

In this paper we give an algorithm for calculating a Nash equilibrium (NE) of the model from. We prove that the algorithm runs in polynomial time in the number of players. The idea is to reduce the network by removing the nodes that are not attacked under any NE, while still keeping all of the possible paths of attack. We identify a subset of defending nodes that we call linkers, which are the nodes that are never attacked in any NE. Once the linkers are removed from the network, the attacker can reach every node by a path of increasing values for the attacker. We use this observation, and we build on the idea for computing NE for linear networks (where the nodes are connected in order of ascending values) from, and we get a polynomial time algorithm that finds a NE of the model for any connected network.

- Network interdiction

  - applications: smuggling goods, detecting nuclear material, disrupting troop movement
  - surveys

  - zero-sum game: evader picks any path, interdictor picks an edge; detected with fixed prob. if edge on path
  - contribution there: reduce LP for zero-sum games to polynomial number of constraints/variables despite possibly exponential evader strategy set

The problem of strategic transportation and interception of unwanted traffic through a network is called network interdiction. In the classic formulation there are two players: an evader, who sends the traffic through the network, and the interceptor, who wants to stop the traffic. Network interdiction has been studied a lot over the past years. Depending on the model, the goal of the evader can be minimizing the length of the path from the source to the sink, avoiding detection by devices that the interdictor places on the edges, or increasing the flow between the source and the sink. Applications of the network interdiction problem go from smuggling goods and detecting nuclear material to disrupting the movement of enemy troops. There are excellent surveys of this type of model.

The literature on NE computation is very large, so we only look at the most closely related works. Prior work considers a zero-sum game model where the evader chooses any path on the graph and the interdictor chooses an edge in the graph. If the edge is on the evader's path, then the evader is detected with a fixed probability assigned to that edge. One contribution of that work is reducing the linear programming problem, which is the classic method for solving zero-sum games, to a polynomial number of constraints and variables, even when the strategy set of the evader is possibly of exponential size.

A model that is closer to ours is the one in, where each of the n defenders chooses whether to protect himself or not. The defenders are connected in a directed weighted graph, and the weights of the edges reflect the probability of being contaminated by the incoming neighbours if they are successfully attacked. Two main settings are considered: in the first the direct attack is the result of a random event (e.g. a pandemic), and in the second the attacks are coordinated by an attacker who wants to maximize the number of infected nodes (e.g. hacker attacks). The authors give a polynomial time algorithm for computing a NE for these models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
International drug trafficking [1,2], disrupting the movement of the enemy troops [3,4], and terrorist attacks [5] involve strategic actors that interact over a network of bilateral connections. One class of scenarios of this type consists of a network of defenders (e.g. countries connected by common borders) and an attacker who attempts to move an undesirable object (e.g. a bomb or a package of drugs) through the network to a targeted node (e.g. a targeted country). Each defender is interested in his own security, but investment in protection spills over to subsequent defenders on the potential routes of attack.

In a recent paper, Bloch, Chatterjee, and Dutta [6] introduce a game theoretic model that captures such scenarios. In the model, an attacker (node 0) and n defenders are all connected in a fixed network. The attacker chooses a target node and an attack path in the network from her location (node 0) to the location of the targeted node. If the attack succeeds, the attacker gains the value assigned to the target node. If successfully attacked, the targeted defender loses his value, while every other node on the path remains intact. To prevent potential losses, every defender can invest in costly protection that increases the probability of stopping a potential attack. An attack can be stopped by any defender on the attack path. Bloch et al. [6] establish the existence of mixed strategy Nash equilibria (NE) in the model and obtain a partial characterization of the NE, as well as a full characterization for networks that form a line. They prove that the set of nodes attacked with positive probability in NE is unique and that, under a certain redefinition, the model has a unique NE. They also provide a set of non-linear equations describing the strategies in a NE when the set of nodes attacked with positive probability is given. Whether this set can be computed efficiently, and hence whether a NE of the model can be computed efficiently, was left as an open question.

We provide an algorithm for calculating a Nash equilibrium (NE) of the model proposed in [6], and we prove that it runs in polynomial time with respect to the number of players. In more detail, we reduce the network by removing the nodes that are not attacked under any NE while maintaining all of the possible paths of attack. We identify a subset of defending nodes, called linkers, which are never attacked in any NE. After the linkers are removed from the network, every node can be reached by the attacker via a path of increasing values for the attacker. Using this observation, and building on the idea presented in [6] for computing NE for linear networks, where the nodes are connected in order of ascending values, we obtain a polynomial time algorithm that finds a NE of the model for any connected network.

The problem of strategic transportation and interception of unwanted traffic through a network is known as network interdiction. In its classic formulation, the problem involves two players: an evader, who sends the traffic through the network, and the interceptor, whose objective is to stop the traffic. Network interdiction has been studied extensively over the past years. In different models, the evader's goal can be minimizing the length of the path from the source to the sink [7], avoiding detection by devices placed by the interdictor on the edges [8], or increasing the flow between the source and the sink [9,4,3]. Applications of network interdiction range from smuggling goods [1,2] and detecting nuclear material [5] to disrupting enemy troop movement [3,4]. See [10] and [11] for excellent surveys of this type of model.

The literature on NE computation is vast, so we restrict attention to the most closely related works. [8] consider a zero-sum game model in which the evader chooses any path on the graph and the interdictor chooses an edge in the graph. If this edge is on the path chosen by the evader, the evader is detected with a fixed probability assigned to the edge. One of the contributions of [8] is to reduce the linear programming problem, the classic method for solving zero-sum games, to a polynomial number of constraints and variables even though the evader's strategy set is of possibly exponential size.

Closer to the model considered in this paper is the model of [12], in which each of the n defenders chooses whether or not to protect himself. The defenders are connected in a directed weighted graph, with edge weights reflecting the probability of being contaminated by incoming neighbours in case they are successfully attacked. Two main settings are considered: in the first, the direct attack results from a random event (e.g. a pandemic); in the second, the attacks are coordinated by an attacker with an incentive to maximize the number of infected nodes (e.g. hacker attacks). The authors propose a polynomial time algorithm for computing a NE for the models they consider.
